img-2715-4760f8ea34.title: Golden arches, translated
img-2715-4760f8ea34.body: This São Paulo Mequi -- Brazil's affectionate nickname for McDonald's -- is reportedly the chain's 1,000th location in the country, tucked into a converted early-1900s mansion from Paulista Avenue's original mansion-row days.

img-2723-9b70c4fb57.title: One horizon, endless city
img-2723-9b70c4fb57.body: Walking the skyline on foot, the concrete sea stretching in every direction -- Brazil starts loud.

img-2725-c11d751263.title: The city as canvas
img-2725-c11d751263.body: A mural-wrapped building near Paulista Avenue -- São Paulo's street-art scene exploded after the city banned outdoor billboards in 2006, clearing the way for muralists like Os Gêmeos and Nina Pandolfo to turn the city into a canvas.

img-2727-a85b9fd07e.body: A Brazilian steak dinner to remember at Figueira Rubaiyat -- built around a massive fig tree in the dining room -- picanha, ribeye, palm heart, and pitu shrimp piled high.
img-2727-a85b9fd07e.title: Dinner under the fig tree

img-2735-28ab2eca22.title: The only way in
img-2735-28ab2eca22.body: Landed at Alta Floresta -- from here, the only way to Cristalino Lodge is by truck, then a transfer onto a boat for the final stretch up the river.

img-0949-7cc238e17d.title: Dwarfed by a tree
img-0949-7cc238e17d.body: Four of us barely wrap around the base of a centuries-old Brazil nut tree, one of the giants of the Cristalino.

dsc00036-171df22a9e.title: Fifteen minutes in
dsc00036-171df22a9e.body: Fifteen minutes into our very first boat tour, and already a Harpy Eagle -- the most powerful raptor in the Americas -- watching us from a branch over the river.

dsc00108-bbffb10b02.title: White against green
dsc00108-bbffb10b02.body: A snowy egret working the shallows along the Cristalino's clear water.

dsc00408-7339a02d29.title: Standing their ground
dsc00408-7339a02d29.body: A troop of spider monkeys shook branches and barked warnings, trying to scare us off their patch of canopy.

dsc00455-f19d422c73.title: A wary eye
dsc00455-f19d422c73.body: One of the spider monkey troop pausing mid-branch, keeping a wary eye on us below. Thumbless, they are built to swing by their tails instead.

dsc00609-6cf622cb46.title: Through the high canopy
dsc00609-6cf622cb46.body: The spider monkey troop moved fast through the treetops -- our guide said some of the younger ones had never seen humans before and were more curious than afraid, pausing to watch us as we watched them.

dsc00870-fe2707a496.title: One more frame
dsc00870-fe2707a496.body: Out on the water at sunset, camera up, chasing the day's last good light.

img-2842-dcb27a4d93.title: Into the canopy
img-2842-dcb27a4d93.body: Our guide leading the way across the canopy walkway, high above the forest floor.

img-2900-e0815cfa58.title: An unbroken sea of green
img-2900-e0815cfa58.body: Sunrise from the Cristalino Lodge observation deck -- an unbroken carpet of rainforest stretching to the horizon.

dsc01309-90853e40f3.title: The tree fills up
dsc01309-90853e40f3.body: Neotropical cormorants and cattle egrets crowd a single tree at dusk, stacking up branch by branch.

img-2788-79afca8ad6.title: The sky catches fire
img-2788-79afca8ad6.body: The sky went orange right as the roost tree filled with birds -- one of the best sunsets of the trip.

img-2797-43aa1fe11c.title: Riding it in
img-2797-43aa1fe11c.body: Heading back to the lodge as the roost tree glowed behind us in the sunset.

dsc01370-ddb01aff26.title: Small things, big eyes
dsc01370-ddb01aff26.body: A tree frog found on low vegetation during a night walk, clinging to a leaf by its adhesive toe pads.

dsc01461-1d7106395b.title: A stingless bee, a bromeliad in bloom
dsc01461-1d7106395b.body: A stingless bee working a pink-coned aechmea in bloom -- one of a thousand tiny scenes at knee height in the Cristalino's understory.

dsc01907-eb96b3b619.title: The otter on the boulder
dsc01907-eb96b3b619.body: A neotropical otter hauled out on a midstream boulder, grabbing fish with its paws -- we watched it catch seven in a row in the Cristalino river.

dsc02014-2c5f2431c2.title: The taricaya's tears
dsc02014-2c5f2431c2.body: Locals call it the taricaya: a yellow-spotted river turtle basking on a rock while butterflies and bees drink its tears, hunting minerals scarce in the Amazon.

dsc02088-774e6f8bcd.title: Boats at rest
dsc02088-774e6f8bcd.body: Lodge boats resting on the water as the forest went quiet for the night.

dsc02142-e5874bf98c.title: The forest exhales
dsc02142-e5874bf98c.body: Another look from the Cristalino Lodge observation deck -- Amazon trees release so much water vapor through transpiration that scientists call the resulting moisture flow a 'flying river'; this is what it looks like at first light, still pooled in the canopy before the sun burns it off.

img-2833-dd8abb0b33.title: Right outside our door
img-2833-dd8abb0b33.body: Returning from a hike, we found a capybara grazing a few feet from our room -- close enough to touch.

img-2858-9f914f72cc.title: Sand and clear water
img-2858-9f914f72cc.body: A quiet stretch of white-sand beach on the Cristalino -- shoes off, feet in the warm current.

dsc02187-97ac82c963.title: The elegant one
dsc02187-97ac82c963.body: A night encounter with an ocelot, the Pantanal's most elegant small cat -- chain-like rosettes smearing into long streaks.

dsc02271-0ee304448c.title: Deer, with bird
dsc02271-0ee304448c.body: A pampas deer doe crossing open grassland with a passenger -- a cattle tyrant riding her back for flushed insects.

dsc02339-de547a705f.title: The Pantanal's emblem
dsc02339-de547a705f.body: A Jabiru stork -- the tallest flying bird in the Americas, and widely considered the Pantanal's own emblem -- pulling a fresh crab from the grass with its great upturned bill.

dsc02472-c6a4b24f7f.title: A cub in daylight
dsc02472-c6a4b24f7f.body: The headline of the trip: a six-month-old jaguar cub trailing close behind its mother, skittish of us in a way she wasn't.

dsc02518-931c84d465.title: Gardener of the forest
dsc02518-931c84d465.body: South America's largest land mammal -- known locally as the Brazilian tapir -- out and browsing in the open at midday. Notoriously shy and difficult to track, this was a rare, clear look at one.

dsc02568-d2b05e28ed.title: An eight-legged crossing
dsc02568-d2b05e28ed.body: A tarantula crossing the track during a safari drive through the Pantanal grounds.

dsc02602-28b6008dba.title: Silhouettes at sunset
dsc02602-28b6008dba.body: A flock of storks cut black against a burning orange Pantanal sunset.

dsc02811-7dfb0b9308.title: Early bird gets the snake
dsc02811-7dfb0b9308.body: Two southern crested caracaras in a tug-of-war over a snake -- technically part of the falcon family, but nothing like a typical falcon: bold, ground-striding opportunists that scavenge as much as they hunt.

dsc02834-b0592de054.title: Ancient and unbothered
dsc02834-b0592de054.body: A yacare caiman resting at the water's edge, close enough to count every scale. Hunted hard for its hide in the 1980s, the species has since rebounded to some 10 million strong across the Pantanal.

dsc02889-8dc3b09536.title: Red, white and black
dsc02889-8dc3b09536.body: A yellow-billed cardinal atop a flowering shrub, crisp red, white and black. The name's a bit of a misnomer -- it's actually a tanager, not a true cardinal.

dsc02921-9e9dd104f6.title: The largest kingfisher alive
dsc02921-9e9dd104f6.body: A ringed kingfisher, the largest kingfisher in the Americas, framed through palm fronds above the water.

dsc03009-4851a7e6ee.title: Jaws ajar
dsc03009-4851a7e6ee.body: Another yacare caiman sunning in the wetland grass, jaws cracked open to cool down.

dsc03020-92020f4b1b.title: Napping in the open
dsc03020-92020f4b1b.body: The world's largest rodent doesn't hurry for anyone — this one stayed stretched out and dozing in the grass, completely unfazed by our jeep.

dsc03028-e5b4bf63ec.title: Waiting for a meal
dsc03028-e5b4bf63ec.body: A trio of lesser yellow-headed vultures waiting on carrion, patient scavengers that quarter low over open country, sniffing out their next meal.

dsc03044-342f12324e.title: The largest parrot alive
dsc03044-342f12324e.body: A bonded pair of the world's largest flying parrot, cobalt from crown to tail, greeting each other at their nest box.

dsc03048-ab8e831ffc.title: Two of a kind
dsc03048-ab8e831ffc.body: A bonded pair of hyacinth macaws -- the world's largest flying parrot, cobalt from crown to tail -- perched together in a tree above the trail.

dsc03126-b2d1854960.title: An armored shuffle
dsc03126-b2d1854960.body: A six-banded armadillo shuffling through the evening grass, backlit by the low sun.

dsc03163-be20f41989.title: Standing on a fence post
dsc03163-be20f41989.body: A burrowing owl -- one that lives underground and hunts by day -- standing tall on a fence post in warm light.

dsc03373-d8e19a4866.title: The continent's largest deer
dsc03373-d8e19a4866.body: A marsh deer buck in full antler -- the continent's largest deer, and one of the Pantanal's Big Five alongside the jaguar, tapir and giant anteater.

dsc03598-28bfb8641d.title: Sneaking closer
dsc03598-28bfb8641d.body: A second jaguar sighting -- this time a pair. The female creeping quietly toward us through the grass, wary but drawing near, the much larger male trailing behind.

dsc03604-75617a4a40.title: A few strides closer
dsc03604-75617a4a40.body: The same jaguar, unbothered by the safari jeep, closing the distance step by step.

dsc03644-76be797401.title: The big male, at rest
dsc03644-76be797401.body: The large male settling into the grass -- a rare, close, calm portrait.

dsc03693-aa0fe4ad17.title: Following her
dsc03693-aa0fe4ad17.body: The male trailing after the female, intent on mating.

img-2943-daaeb5aadd.title: Wetland gold
img-2943-daaeb5aadd.body: The Pantanal's wetland lagoon glowing gold at sunset -- a quiet close to a wildlife-packed day.

img-2987-03121b254a.title: Copacabana, finally
img-2987-03121b254a.body: The mountains behind, the Atlantic in front -- our first view of Rio from the hotel balcony.

img-3012-8e94da00d6.title: The city lit up gold
img-3012-8e94da00d6.body: Rio's bay and skyline lit gold from the top of Sugarloaf Mountain at sunset.

img-3036-125f159bc3.title: At the feet of Christ the Redeemer
img-3036-125f159bc3.body: The whole family at the base of Christ the Redeemer, high above the city on Corcovado.

img-3045-pano-e8f1bf4365.title: Rio, spread out below
img-3045-pano-e8f1bf4365.body: A sweeping panorama from Corcovado -- beaches, bay, and mountains laid out in one frame.

img-3048-9ef580c62e.title: Together at the top
img-3048-9ef580c62e.body: The family at the summit platform, Christ the Redeemer towering just behind us.

img-3055-3e5a6402a5.title: Under open arms
img-3055-3e5a6402a5.body: Standing right at the base of Christ the Redeemer atop Corcovado, looking straight up at its outstretched arms.

img-3099-fbb79ec833.title: Copacabana at last light
img-3099-fbb79ec833.body: Sunset from the rooftop bar at the Emiliano, our hotel on Copacabana -- the first thing we saw of Rio, with the mountains behind and the Atlantic stretched out in front.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-27-479a6587.title: Ian, inside the machine
por-maycon-nunes-photography-27-479a6587.body: Ian wearing one of the front-of-parade fantasias -- the entire thing rides on one person, all the way down the Sambadrome.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-51-a52e69a1.title: Zach in the wardrobe room
por-maycon-nunes-photography-51-a52e69a1.body: Racks of real parade costumes and an open invitation to put one on. Zach's green-and-gold fantasia came with a matching crown and a lot more weight than it looks.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-112-971c4c9.title: A crash course in Carnaval
por-maycon-nunes-photography-112-971c4c9.body: Carnaval Experience, a working samba-school warehouse in Rio where the floats, the sets, and the fantasias are built. An afternoon learning how a parade gets made, ending with a turn each on the surdo and the caixa alongside the crew.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-144-aa3bc0d.title: The steps that took twenty years
por-maycon-nunes-photography-144-aa3bc0d.body: Escadaria Selarón: 215 steps that the Chilean artist Jorge Selarón tiled by hand from 1990 until his death in 2013, using tiles sent to him from more than 60 countries.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-148-eee1373.title: All four of us, mid-staircase
por-maycon-nunes-photography-148-eee1373.body: Escadaria Selarón, the Lapa steps -- 215 of them, tiled by hand by the Chilean artist Jorge Selarón from 1990 until his death in 2013, with tiles sent to him from more than 60 countries. The red, yellow and green running the whole length were his tribute to Brazil.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-158-5d1c81c.title: Ian and Zach on the mosaic
por-maycon-nunes-photography-158-5d1c81c.body: The brothers stopped partway up. Every step is its own mosaic, pieced from more than 2,000 tiles, and no two of them quite match.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-243-0ef6bb4.title: Christ, from across the valley
por-maycon-nunes-photography-243-0ef6bb4.body: Mirante Dona Marta, high on the edge of Tijuca Forest -- the classic view of Christ the Redeemer without standing underneath it.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-247-11de0d9.title: The walk-and-talk
por-maycon-nunes-photography-247-11de0d9.body: Our photographer's favorite trick: keep walking, don't look at the camera. Corcovado handles the rest of the frame.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-260-bf98f6c.title: Zach, Sugarloaf across the bay
por-maycon-nunes-photography-260-bf98f6c.body: Zach on the wall at Dona Marta, where the whole of Botafogo Bay opens up -- Pão de Açúcar, Sugarloaf Mountain, standing out of the water at the harbor mouth.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-283-f34b185.title: Through the branches
por-maycon-nunes-photography-283-f34b185.body: Christ the Redeemer -- 30 meters of soapstone on a 710-meter granite peak -- framed by the Atlantic forest that still covers Corcovado.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-293-a3cbf13.title: Backlit at golden hour
por-maycon-nunes-photography-293-a3cbf13.body: The same statue four hours and one mountain later, shot from Morro da Urca as the sun went down behind Corcovado.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-301-ca839d8.title: Sunset from the halfway stop
por-maycon-nunes-photography-301-ca839d8.body: Morro da Urca is the first of the cable car's two stages -- 220 meters up, with Flamengo, the Aterro, and the Rio-Niterói bridge laid out behind.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-315-395219b.title: Under the second cable
por-maycon-nunes-photography-315-395219b.body: On Morro da Urca, with Sugarloaf mountain and the cable car behind.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-327-4bab5f0.title: The four of us, and the loaf
por-maycon-nunes-photography-327-4bab5f0.body: Portuguese traders called it Pão de Açúcar -- sugarloaf -- after the conical clay molds that refined sugar was shipped in.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-335-1eb3f2b.title: The cable line down
por-maycon-nunes-photography-335-1eb3f2b.body: The run back to Urca strung across an orange sky, Botafogo's mooring field below and the Tijuca ridge cut flat against the light.

por-maycon-nunes-photography-340-f2f7b79.title: Everyone waits for the lights
por-maycon-nunes-photography-340-f2f7b79.body: Blue hour on Morro da Urca -- Botafogo's curve, the Aterro do Flamengo, and the Serra dos Órgãos far off across Guanabara Bay.
